answer.rationale: 1. The finance mandate is binding. The incumbent has explicitly refused to reopen price this cycle, so renew_incumbent and negotiate_terms both cannot reach the 18% cut without additional levers I do not have capacity to build in 14 days. This rules out two directions immediately. 2. defer_decision is attractive under memory_c5, but c5 deferred a non-critical renewal onto month-to-month terms. Here the contract does not auto-renew and the assembly line is at 94% with no buffer; deferral here risks a delivery gap, which violates the no-increased-delivery-risk constraint. 3. add_second_source is the pattern from memory_c3, but that memory addressed a constrained component with a single-point-of-failure risk. The current binding constraint is cost, not supply continuity, and I have capacity for only one decision; a second source adds cost rather than removing it. 4. That leaves switch_primary_vendor. The decisive uncertainty is whether the low-cost vendor can actually deliver reliably and invoice accurately at scale, because a switch that meets the 18% mandate but disrupts the 94%-utilization line would trade one risk for a worse one. memory_c2 is the only memory that records a prior switch to this same low-cost vendor, and it reports quick onboarding and accurate invoicing. Verifying it tells me whether that experience was real and recent enough to rely on for a 14-day transition. 5. If memory_c2 confirms as stated, I execute the switch. If the archive shows the quote was conditional, the onboarding was longer than remembered, or accuracy issues surfaced later, I fall back to renew_incumbent at the existing price and absorb the finance variance into the next review, because delivery risk to a 94%-loaded line is the harder failure to recover from. 6. Downsides I am flagging explicitly: switching concentrates supply on a single low-cost vendor, recreating the single-point-of-failure pattern that memory_c3 was designed to remove. The correct follow-up for the next review cycle is to qualify a second source, not to treat this switch as a permanent structure. Preserving that optionality means I should negotiate the new contract with short notice-period termination and no exclusivity lock-in, which costs nothing now and keeps the next cycle's choices open.
